literal: Great Wei answered the age and embraced all within the seas.
idiomatic: Great Wei rose to its season and took the realm within the four seas.

literal: Emperor Xiaowen the Filial and Cultured, with sage wisdom ruling Heaven, restored the old canons.
idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowen, sage and cultured, ruled with heaven's wit and restored the old canons.

literal: He then ordered the former Supervisor of the Palace Secretariat Gao Lu to proclaim widely in the Confucian schools, search out the Music Bureau, take the Six Classics as basis and consult the histories of the states, cut the inch from millet, and balance the old statutes of Zhou and Han.
idiomatic: He ordered former Secretariat Supervisor Gao Lu to scour the schools, recover the Music Bureau, ground the work in the Six Classics and state histories, cut the inch from millet grain, and align Zhou and Han measure.

literal: But as the cloud-frame capital was still moving, the work was not yet complete.
idiomatic: The capital was still on the move; the work was not finished.

literal: The emperor's wise thought was profound and abstruse; consulting classics and records, he used one millet's size to form the whole body, took it as standard for the foot, and proclaimed and enacted it.
idiomatic: His thought ran deep; from the classics he took one millet-grain as module for the whole foot, made it law, and proclaimed it.

literal: By the Zhengshi era the former Director of Imperial Music Gongsun Chong on his own set up a scheme, making twelve millet for the inch and separately forging measure and pitch, fixing the law and casting bells.
idiomatic: In Zhengshi, former Director of Imperial Music Gongsun Chong devised his own scheme—twelve millet to the inch—new measure, new pitch, new bells.

literal: All were finished in one direction; he memorialized requesting inspection and trial.
idiomatic: When all was ready he asked for trial before the court.

literal: At the time an edict ordered Grand Director of Imperial Sacrifices Fang to gather the court's worthies, since Chong's work was done, and debate whether it was acceptable.
idiomatic: The throne told Grand Director Fang to assemble the court's experts and judge Chong's finished work.

literal: Fang doubted that Chong's measure differed from the prior dynasty's, examined its makers against classics and histories and found further discrepancy, judged the forging thinly grounded, and held it should not be enacted.
idiomatic: Fang found Chong's foot unlike the prior dynasty's, checked makers against the classics, found the basis thin, and said it must not pass.

literal: At that time Director Zhao, Prince of Qinghe Yi, and others held Chong's forging mistaken and unlike the Rites of Zhou; they memorialized that Fang should remake according to the Rites of Zhou, and when finished compare measures and follow whichever was better.
idiomatic: Zhao, Prince Yi of Qinghe, and others said Chong erred against the Zhou Rites and urged Fang to remake by Zhou measure, then compare and take the better.

literal: But Fang held that the prior dynasty's measure accorded with the ancient canon.
idiomatic: Fang held the old foot already matched antiquity.

literal: He therefore followed the earlier edict, cut the inch from millet, and presented it to the court to trim metal and stone.
idiomatic: He followed the earlier edict, cut the inch from millet, and presented it to tune bells and stones.

literal: Among debaters at the time many said Fang was right; only Yellow Gate Attendant Sun Huiwei sided with Chong.
idiomatic: Most debaters sided with Fang; only Sun Huiwei, Yellow Gate Attendant, backed Chong.

literal: The two paths diverged and were repeatedly examined in debate.
idiomatic: Two paths diverged; debate ran again and again.

literal: And Director Zhao favored Fang's forging.
idiomatic: Director Zhao favored what Fang had made.

literal: After Chong died, Huiwei also forged a foot, still claiming support.
idiomatic: After Chong died, Huiwei forged another foot and still claimed his own side.

literal: [9] Compared with Chong's foot, they contradicted each other.
idiomatic: [9] Laid beside Chong's foot, the two measures contradicted each other.

literal: Measuring and checking, two or three points favored Fang as correct.
idiomatic: On measurement, two or three tests favored Fang.

literal: But Kuang of the Masters of Writing memorialized that Liu's and Sun's two feet, long and short leaning against each other, when examined against the two pitch laws contained markedly different capacities.
idiomatic: Kuang of the Masters of Writing wrote that Liu's foot and Sun's foot tilted against each other, and when tested against the two pitch laws their capacities diverged sharply.

literal: He said to take the middle millet and compare the two houses, declaring both divergent with no middle ground [10], establishing his own path and asking for judgment.
idiomatic: He proposed a middle millet, compared both schools, found neither sound [10], set his own path, and asked the court to decide.

literal: Among debaters at the time some sided with Kuang.
idiomatic: Some debaters then sided with Kuang.

literal: The two paths clashed and were not settled at once.
idiomatic: The quarrel collided and was not settled.

literal: Zhao also said that weights, bushels, dou, and feet had been promulgated long since; what was now debated could hardly match the prior intent.
idiomatic: Zhao said weights, bushels, and feet had long been law—today's quarrel could not match the old intent.

literal: One should respectfully follow the prior dynasty's old foot as fixed.
idiomatic: The prior dynasty's foot should stand as fixed.

literal: From then on Kuang and Zhao spoke harshly in the chief seat, voices and faces adding against each other; high and low lost their constant order, and clamor no longer kept ritual sequence.
idiomatic: After that Kuang and Zhao shouted across the chief seat; rank lost its order and debate lost its ritual.

literal: Kuang memorialized again in columns, holding his own ten points true and Fang's ten false.
idiomatic: Kuang listed charges again: his ten points true, Fang's ten false.

literal: He also said: "Zhao earlier received the edict to supervise with Fang, planning the names of bells and stones, hoping to spread the reputation of making them."
idiomatic: He wrote, "Zhao was edicted to supervise with Fang, to name the bells and stones and win the fame of their making."

literal: He relied on the dignity of the pivot-scale and borrowed his maternal clan's power; grant and denial followed his heart, praise and blame were his own.
idiomatic: He leaned on the minister's scale and his kin's power; grant and denial, praise and blame, were his alone.

literal: He curried favor with Liu Fang, blocked my business, greeted those who echoed his power with kind words, and raged at those who checked against the classics.
idiomatic: He favored Liu Fang, blocked my work, flattered those who echoed him, and raged at those who held to the classics.

literal: Though he had not yet turned deer into horses or moved heaven and shifted the sun, he truly made reserved scholars draw up their breath at their seats and men who kept the Way bite their tongues at the mats.
idiomatic: He had not yet turned deer to horses or moved heaven—but reserved scholars held their breath at court and honest men bit their tongues at the feast.

literal: He also said: "Fang once competed with Chong and always said he made things himself; now debating with me he suddenly calls on the prior dynasty."
idiomatic: He added, "Fang once fought Chong and called every measure his own; now, debating me, he hides behind the prior dynasty."

literal: Was it not that he first said it could be done and wished to take it for himself, then knowing it wrong pushed it onto the prior dynasty?
idiomatic: First he said his scheme would work and meant to claim it; when error showed, he pushed it on the old emperors.

literal: This is far from the bearing of a great minister and deeply fails the duty of a subordinate.
idiomatic: That is not how great ministers behave, nor how subordinates should serve.

literal: If I again examine before the powerful minister and the partial hand that skewed measure, I shall surely lose my feet within the inner court and embrace jade outside among men."
idiomatic: Before power's skewed hand I shall lose my feet in court and carry jade in the street."

literal: Wild words ran at will and showed plainly through court and market.
idiomatic: His wild words rang through court and market.

literal: Yet Kuang's duty was intake and delivery, and remonstrance was his place; weights, bushels, and measure were precisely his office.
idiomatic: Yet Kuang's duty was intake and remonstrance—and weights and measures were his office.

literal: If he had his own view and could judge right and wrong, he should have led with righteous argument early and distinguished the doubts—why keep silent and follow, not speaking one word, and only after Fang's work was done utter these words?
idiomatic: If he truly saw the flaw he should have spoken when it mattered—why stay silent until Fang succeeded, then cry fraud?

literal: Considering Fang's talent and learning, it cannot be hung with Kuang's; the shallow and deep of their views should not be matched.
idiomatic: Fang's learning towers above Kuang's; their depth cannot be compared.

literal: Now he speaks only at the end—I fear this comes from the heart [11], borrowing another's wit to seek empty reputation.
idiomatic: Now he speaks late—I fear vanity [11], borrowing others' wit for hollow fame.

literal: Moreover Kuang's memorial said: "The bronze weight he relies on is shaped like the ancient record—clearly Han work, not a separate forging of Mang."
idiomatic: Kuang also said his bronze weight matched the ancient record—clearly Han, not Mang's new forge.

literal: And examining the weight's inscription: "The Yellow Emperor's first ancestor—his virtue spread to Yu; Yu the Emperor's first ancestor—his virtue spread to Xin."
idiomatic: The inscription read: "Yellow Emperor's first ancestor, virtue to Yu; Yu the Emperor's first ancestor, virtue to Xin."

literal: If Mang assisted Han in his time, how could there be an inscription with the false name Xin?
idiomatic: If Mang served Han, why would the inscription bear the false name Xin?

literal: Searching further Mang's biography: when Mang held the regency he at once changed Han institutions.
idiomatic: Mang's biography says that in regency he changed Han institutions at once.

literal: Checking the two proofs, it is clear it is not a Han weight.
idiomatic: The two proofs show it is no Han weight.

literal: He also said: "What Fang forged is again shorter than the prior dynasty's foot."
idiomatic: He also said Fang's foot falls short of the prior dynasty's.

literal: Your subject has compared them—the weight agrees exactly.
idiomatic: I compared them—the weight matches exactly.

literal: He further said: "Fang's foot differs from the Qianjin weir."
idiomatic: He further said Fang's foot differs from the Qianjin weir mark.

literal: Your subject again measured and compared and thereupon saw the difference.
idiomatic: I measured again and saw the difference.

literal: Two or three floating excesses—hard to take as standard.
idiomatic: Two or three loose points—too weak to serve as standard.

literal: He also said: "Together they built a false edge, recklessly made suspected forms, and lodged it on the prior dynasty, saying it was not their own making."
idiomatic: He also charged them with forging doubt and pinning it on the prior dynasty, saying it was not their work.

literal: Your subject finds this deceit lies in Kuang, not in Fang.
idiomatic: The deceit is Kuang's, not Fang's.

literal: How so?
idiomatic: Why?

literal: Fang was first edicted to specialize in forging bells and pitch; the excellence of pipes and reeds was his to trim—weights, bushels, and measure were originally not his affair.
idiomatic: Fang was edicted to make bells and pitch; pipes were his—but weights and bushels were never his charge.

literal: Earlier the Secretariat sought Fang's measure and Fang replied in a document: "Following the prior dynasty's promulgated new foot, again applying lower millet without further increase or decrease—only to tune bells and pitch and adjust inches and parts."
idiomatic: When the Secretariat asked his measure, Fang replied: "I follow the prior dynasty's promulgated foot, lower millet unchanged—only tuning bells and pitch."

literal: Checking Kuang's forging—it was one year after that document; on that day Kuang had not yet disputed with Fang and this document already existed—how could it be fraud?
idiomatic: Kuang forged his measure a year later; that day he had not yet quarreled with Fang—the document already existed; where is the fraud?

literal: Considering Chong forged the inch with twelve millet accumulated—all knew it in common;
idiomatic: All knew Chong made the inch from twelve millet;

literal: while Fang's inch used only ten millet—both likewise followed prior edicts.
idiomatic: Fang's inch used only ten—both cited prior edicts.

literal: Making the inch from millet, head and tail clear in the record—how could there be rash wish to take it for oneself?
idiomatic: The millet-to-inch chain is explicit in the record—who could seize it for himself?

literal: Zhao's post stands at the right hand; the hundred officials look to him—word, act, movement, and stillness must match what all watch.
idiomatic: Zhao stands at the minister's right hand; the hundred officials watch him—word and deed must match their gaze.

literal: If he relies on power to curry favor, fraudulently lodges on a prior edict, and would turn deer to horses or shift sun and move heaven, he is Zhao Gao of Wei—how can he govern things?
idiomatic: If he curries power, fakes old edicts, and would turn deer to horses or move heaven, he is Wei's Zhao Gao—how can he govern?

literal: If Zhao has none of this, Kuang has slandered the chief minister and mocked the bright age.
idiomatic: If Zhao did none of this, Kuang has slandered the chief minister and mocked a bright age.

literal: Should there be turning-deer affairs in the midst of debate;
idiomatic: Should debate hold turning-deer affairs;

literal: at the moment of yes and no, light words of cutting off one's feet?
idiomatic: at the moment of judgment, talk of cutting off one's feet?

literal: Zhao Gao's false confusion belonged to declining Qin;
idiomatic: Zhao Gao's fraud belonged to fallen Qin;

literal: Bian He embracing jade met violent Chu in its time.
idiomatic: Bian He embracing jade met brutal Chu in its season.

literal: How should a court so teeming have such slander!
idiomatic: Why should so teeming a court hear such slander!

literal: Blocking and confusing the court's hearing is insubordination in the extreme—please forbid both Zhao and Kuang from the Masters of Writing, push to the root, and hand to the Court Director for sentencing.
idiomatic: They block the court's ear—insubordination at its height—bar Zhao and Kuang from the Masters of Writing and send both to the Court Director for sentence.

literal: An edict said "Approved."
idiomatic: The edict said, "Approved."

literal: The relevant offices memorialized that Kuang had slandered Zhao and sentenced Kuang to death.
idiomatic: The offices ruled Kuang had slandered Zhao and sought death.

literal: Shizong remitted death and reduced him to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
idiomatic: Shizong remitted death and made him Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.

literal: He was also made concurrent Grand Director of the Imperial Clan and sent out as Inspector of Yan Province.
idiomatic: He was also made Grand Director of the Imperial Clan and sent out as Inspector of Yan Province.

literal: As Kuang was about to depart, the emperor received him in the Eastern Hall and comforted and encouraged him.
idiomatic: As Kuang set out, the emperor received him in the Eastern Hall and comforted him.

literal: Kuang still spoke of measure, feet, metal, and stone as the great warp of the state; though earlier the Southern Terrace had impeached him, he was still allowed further debate—if debate came, he wished permission to hurry to court for a time.
idiomatic: Kuang still called measure and bells the state's great warp; though the Southern Terrace had impeached him, he might debate again—if debate came, he asked leave to hurry to court.

literal: Shizong said: "Liu Fang's learning towers over a generation; he is deep and clear in ancient precedent—what he relies on."
idiomatic: Shizong said, "Liu Fang's learning towers over his age; he knows antiquity—what he relies on."

literal: With the prior dynasty's foot the inch exceeds by one millet—how can he again say it is the prior dynasty's intent?"
idiomatic: His foot's inch exceeds the prior dynasty's by one millet—how can he call that the old intent?"

literal: [12] Yan Province is already what you grasp without warrant; when later debate comes, why wait to come to the capital?"
idiomatic: [12] Yan is already beyond your warrant; when debate comes, why return to the capital?"

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Suzong's reign he entered as Censor-in-Chief.
idiomatic: At Suzong's opening he entered as Censor-in-Chief.

literal: Kuang was severe in impeachment; he first memorialized against Yu Zhong, then impeached Gao Cong and others for removal—the Empress Dowager Ling permitted none of it.
idiomatic: Kuang impeached fiercely—first Yu Zhong, then Gao Cong—the Empress Dowager permitted none.

literal: Because it went against her heart in punishing what she hated, and fearing Kuang would resign, she wished to reward and settle him—he was advanced to General Who Pacifies the South, later added General Who Guards the East.
idiomatic: It crossed her will; fearing he would quit, she promoted him—first General Who Pacifies the South, then General Who Guards the East.

literal: Kuang repeatedly asked to remake weights and measures without end; thereupon an edict said: "Careful weight and examined measure are canon from of old; fixing chapters and changing calendars are good rules of past generations."
idiomatic: Kuang would not stop asking to remake measure; an edict said, "Careful weight and examined measure are ancient canon; fixing chapters and changing calendars are old good rules."

literal: Kuang of the imperial clan is worthy and bright and has long kept his mind on this; he may gather Confucian worthies again and test and decide in season.
idiomatic: Kuang of the clan is worthy and has long studied this; let him gather scholars and decide in season.

literal: He must make the scales of weight attain the center and let inch and pitch pipe not err."
idiomatic: Let the scales hit true center and inch and pitch pipe never miss."

literal: Another edict said: "The former Prince Shang of Guangping, Luohou, sprang from Emperor Gongzong; he died young in his prime; the state was abolished and sacrifice cut off—suddenly he was not sacrificed."
idiomatic: Another edict said, "Prince Shang Luohou sprang from Gongzong, died young, and left no heir—the line broke and sacrifice ceased."

literal: Kuang was close as a son in private succession for years [13]; he should plant the wall of the realm and forever be bedrock—he may specially inherit the princely title and be enfeoffed Prince of Dongping."
idiomatic: Kuang stood to him as a son for years [13]; let him be bedrock of the realm—inherit specially as Prince of Dongping."

literal: When Kuang's forged measure was finished, he asked to gather court gentlemen to debate and fix right and wrong.
idiomatic: When Kuang's measure was done, he asked the court to judge right and wrong.

literal: An edict referred it to the Secretariat, Masters of Writing, Three Offices, and Nine Columns to debate and report.
idiomatic: The edict sent it to Secretariat, Masters of Writing, Three Offices, and Nine Columns for debate.

literal: Grand Preceptor Prince Yong of Gaoyang and others debated: "We consider that Emperor Gaozu created and reformed weight and measure and it was fixed; Kuang's new forging has slight discrepancy."
idiomatic: Prince Yong of Gaoyang and others wrote, "Gaozu fixed weight and measure; Kuang's new foot diverges slightly."

literal: Moreover Kuang says the measure he forged does not differ from the Han Monograph's Mang weight and bushel.
idiomatic: Kuang says his foot matches the Han Monograph's Mang weight and bushel.

literal: Also Jin Secretariat Supervisor Xun Xu said that from Later Han to Wei the foot was longer than antiquity by more than four parts.
idiomatic: Jin's Xun Xu said that from Later Han to Wei the foot ran more than four parts longer than antiquity.

literal: Thereupon according to the Rites of Zhou they accumulated millet to raise measure, took only the ancient jade pitch pipes and bells, and thereupon corrected them.
idiomatic: By the Zhou Rites they raised measure from millet, took ancient jade pitch pipes and bells, and corrected them.

literal: Searching out what Xu forged, the foot and what Emperor Gaozu fixed were in hairs and hairs nearly the same.
idiomatic: Xu's foot and Gaozu's foot differed only by hairs.

literal: Also Attendant-in-Chief Cui Guang obtained the ancient elephant foot-rule; at the time it too was approved for debate and ordered enacted.
idiomatic: Cui Guang, Attendant-in-Chief, also found the ancient elephant foot-rule; the court approved it for use.

literal: Looking up to Emperor Xiaowen the Filial and Cultured, his virtue passed prior kings, his keen brightness shone below—an unerased pattern, affairs hard to change.
idiomatic: Xiaowen's virtue passed prior kings; his pattern is not to be lightly changed.

literal: We your subjects jointly debate and ask to stop Kuang's deliberation and forever follow the prior emperor's system."
idiomatic: We jointly ask to stop Kuang's debate and forever follow the prior emperor's system."

literal: The edict followed it.
idiomatic: The edict agreed.

literal: Whenever Kuang had a memorial request, Director Prince Cheng of Ren City often seized and blocked it; Kuang was narrow inside and grew inwardly unequal.
idiomatic: Whenever Kuang memorialized, Director Prince Cheng of Rencheng blocked him; Kuang, narrow by nature, seethed inwardly.

literal: The coffin he had first built still stood in a monk's temple; he again prepared the affair, intending to attack Cheng.
idiomatic: The coffin he had built still stood in a temple; he prepared again to attack Cheng.

literal: Cheng knew it fairly well.
idiomatic: Cheng knew it well enough.

literal: Later as he was going to the ministry he met Kuang; their outriders struck each other; court and market were appalled.
idiomatic: Going to the ministry he met Kuang; their escorts collided; court and market gaped.

literal: Cheng thereupon memorialized more than thirty charges against Kuang; the Court Director sentenced him to death.
idiomatic: Cheng memorialized more than thirty crimes; the Court Director sentenced Kuang to death.
